newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Japan shows interest in tough S.African car sector.
newsitem.headline: Japan shows interest in tough S.African car sector.

text.p: Japanese interest in South Africa's car industry is more a symptom of tough market conditions than a sign of the sector's robust health, analysts said on Wednesday.

Toyota Motor Corp paid 446 million rand for a 27.8 percent stake in Toyota South Africa Ltd last October. Last week it emerged that Automakers Ltd, with links to Nissan and Fiat, is also lining up an international investor.
Fiat quicky denied it had any intention to take a stake and all signs now point to Nissan.
"There are very few people who think the deal isn't being struck with Nissan," said one analyst who declined to be identified.

Automakers and Nissan have declined to confirm or deny the rumours which surfaced last Thursday. The talk quickly flushed two cautionary statements from Automakers as its stock raced ahead -- prompting a Securities Regulation Panel investigation into possible insider trading.
But analysts said they thought it unlikely that the Japanese had made the first approach and were probably responding to a call from players facing stiff competition in the local market.
"A lot of this has come from the South African side where they are basically saying 'help us'," said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell analyst Richard Armitage.

After four years of successive growth, the umbrella National Association of Automobile Manufacturers of South Africa is predicting a drop in new car sales in 1997 as interest rates remain high, keeping a tight grip on consumers' purse strings.

The industry has also suffered from lower duties on foreign cars and components, triggering a flood of imports. In 1995 the industry offered 270 different models, of which 60 were imports, but in 1996 it was about 330, with 120 coming from overseas.
The result has been pressure on prices and fierce competition in the local market.

Automakers, which plans to delist from the Johannesburg Stock Exchange as it brings in a partner, said the tough trading conditions since it floated in October 1995, were unlikely to improve in the medium term.

The selling price of vehicles has in some cases been capped, gross margins have fallen as the entry level to market has dropped, increased competition and higher interest rates are just some of the industry's catalogue of woes.
But analysts said that despite the grim conditions, deals such as Toyota's -- and the possible Nissan scheme -- offer the overseas firms some advantages.

Synergies in component transfers will show clear benefits and South Africa, with a developed financial and industrial infrastructure, offers a springboard to the emerging markets of the rest of the region.
"They could well be looking at other southern African countries. South Africa is often seen as a springboard to investment," one analyst said.

Other market watchers said the importance of the rest of southern Africa could be overestimated as demand in the area's developing economies was still small. One said volumes sold in the region would be only 5-10 percent of those in South Africa.
Japan has been more reluctant to invest in South Africa than have been other Asian nations like Malaysia, which has poured cash into the country since its first all-race elections in 1994.

Toyota senior managing director Shinji Sakai said his firm's deal was in direct reponse to President Nelson Mandela's request for more Japanese investment, but analysts said Tokyo's interest in the car industry was a result of unique circumstances and unlikely to kickstart other investments.
"It is industry-specific. I don't think it is the start of a trend," Armitage said.
